certification.name: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional

domains.name: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance

tasks.name: Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations.
Design and implement enterprise integration architectures.
Implement application integration patterns and development tools.

domains.name: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications

concepts.name: Build autonomous and multi-agent systems with memory
concepts.description: Design agent systems with appropriate session state, durable memory, multi-agent collaboration, and standardized agent-tool interaction patterns such as MCP.

concepts.name: Implement structured agent reasoning
concepts.description: Use explicit reasoning-and-action loops such as ReAct and controlled orchestration when a problem must be decomposed across multiple steps.

concepts.name: Safeguard autonomous workflows
concepts.description: Use stopping conditions, timeouts, least-privilege IAM, circuit breakers, budgets, and other controls to bound agent behavior.

concepts.name: Coordinate specialized models
concepts.description: Use model selection, specialized FMs, ensembles, or aggregation only when combining capabilities improves the task enough to justify added cost and latency.

concepts.name: Add human collaboration and approval
concepts.description: Use human review, approval, and feedback collection for uncertain, sensitive, or high-impact agent decisions.

concepts.name: Implement reliable agent tools
concepts.description: Define tool schemas and behaviors clearly, validate parameters, handle errors, and scope permissions so tool calls are reliable and safe.

concepts.name: Host and consume MCP tool servers
concepts.description: Use Lambda for lightweight stateless MCP servers or ECS/containers for more complex and long-lived tool services, with consistent MCP clients.

concepts.name: Choose an inference deployment mode
concepts.description: Match serverless/on-demand, Provisioned Throughput, or SageMaker endpoint deployment to traffic, customization, latency, and cost needs.

concepts.name: Size LLM serving infrastructure
concepts.description: Account for GPU/accelerator memory, model size, token processing, batching, and concurrency when hosting models yourself.

concepts.name: Cascade models for cost and latency
concepts.description: Route easy tasks to smaller models and escalate only when confidence, complexity, or policy requires a stronger model.

concepts.name: Connect FMs to enterprise environments
concepts.description: Use APIs, event-driven integration, and synchronization patterns to connect GenAI capabilities with legacy and enterprise systems while controlling coupling.

concepts.name: Enhance existing applications with GenAI
concepts.description: Use API Gateway, Lambda, EventBridge, and microservice/webhook patterns to add FM capabilities to existing business applications.

concepts.name: Federate identity and enforce least privilege
concepts.description: Use identity federation, RBAC, and least-privilege API/model/data permissions so enterprise identities receive only authorized GenAI capabilities.

concepts.name: Design hybrid and edge GenAI integrations
concepts.description: Use Outposts, Wavelength, and secure hybrid routing when data locality, jurisdiction, or edge-latency requirements constrain where processing occurs.

concepts.name: Build GenAI CI/CD and gateway architectures
concepts.description: Automate code/prompt/config tests, security scans, evaluation gates, deployment and rollback, and centralize model access with a governed abstraction or gateway.

concepts.name: Invoke FMs synchronously and asynchronously
concepts.description: Use direct Bedrock APIs for interactive calls and queues/workflows for long-running or decoupled processing.

concepts.name: Stream model responses
concepts.description: Use ConverseStream or other streaming response patterns with WebSockets, SSE, or chunked transfer to reduce perceived latency.

concepts.name: Handle throttling and transient API failures
concepts.description: Use exponential backoff, jitter, rate limiting, retries, fallback, and tracing for reliable model calls.

concepts.name: Route requests to the right model
concepts.description: Use static, rules-based, or intelligent routing based on modality, complexity, tenant, latency, cost, and quality requirements.

concepts.name: Integrate GenAI with application APIs
concepts.description: Handle request validation, streaming, timeouts, quotas, and retry behavior at API boundaries.

concepts.name: Build front-end and workflow integrations
concepts.description: Use Amplify, OpenAPI-based clients, Prompt Flows, and AWS serverless services to connect user experiences to GenAI workflows.

concepts.name: Automate document and workflow processing
concepts.description: Use Lambda, Step Functions, and Bedrock Data Automation or related services to coordinate extraction and generative processing.

concepts.name: Use Amazon Q Developer in development workflows
concepts.description: Use Q Developer for coding assistance, explanation, troubleshooting, and productivity while keeping normal review and security practices.

concepts.name: Compose agent and workflow frameworks
concepts.description: Choose Strands, Agent Squad, Step Functions, or prompt chaining based on autonomy, control, and orchestration needs.

concepts.name: Trace application failures across services
concepts.description: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray, traces, and developer tooling to correlate model, API, Lambda, and downstream failures.

questions.prompt: An autonomous support agent can issue refunds and query order data. A refund can create financial loss, so tool use must be reliable and bounded. Choose the strongest design decision at each stage.

steps.prompt: How should the refund capability be exposed to the agent?

choices.label: A narrow typed tool with validated parameters, explicit limits, and least-privilege credentials
A general shell command with production credentials
Execute any free-form model text as code
Give the model an unrestricted administrative API token

steps.prompt: What should happen for refunds above the business risk threshold?

choices.label: Require human approval before the high-impact tool action executes
Store the request in long-term memory and execute automatically
Ask two agents and execute if either says yes

steps.prompt: Which state should be persisted long term?

choices.label: Only selected durable facts the policy says are useful and appropriate to retain
Every prompt, hidden reasoning trace, credential, and tool response forever
No state at all, including required audit identifiers
Customer passwords so future calls are easier

steps.prompt: What best validates the design before broad rollout?

choices.label: Tool-schema/error tests, permission-boundary tests, approval-path tests, and adversarial/prompt-injection scenarios

questions.explanation: High-impact agent actions need external controls, not just careful prompting. A narrow typed tool constrains inputs and permissions; human approval gates actions whose consequence exceeds policy; memory should retain only deliberately selected durable context; and validation must exercise errors, permissions, approval bypass attempts, and adversarial instructions. More agents or a lower temperature do not create an authorization boundary.
hints: Treat the model as a planner/requester; privileged execution still needs deterministic controls.

questions.prompt: Complete the inference-deployment table. Type the deployment mode that best fits each traffic/customization requirement.

need.template: Traffic is variable and the team wants managed Bedrock inference without reserving model capacity.
Traffic is sustained/predictable and the team wants reserved Bedrock model capacity.
A custom-hosted model needs endpoint-level infrastructure/scaling control.

questions.explanation: Bedrock On-Demand is the managed default for variable traffic without reserved capacity; Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity for sustained predictable demand; and a SageMaker endpoint is appropriate when the application needs a custom model or more serving-infrastructure control. Choosing a mode is a traffic/capability/cost decision—not simply picking the most expensive option for every production workload.
hints: Look for the clues: variable managed demand, reserved managed capacity, or custom endpoint control.

error_codes.description: One or more typed answers did not match an accepted answer.
One or more required blanks were left empty.

questions.prompt: Build the responsibilities of an enterprise GenAI integration. Assign the component/pattern that directly fits each role.

slots.label: Authenticate/federate users and give the workload least-privilege AWS access
Expose a stable application API boundary instead of coupling clients directly to model details
Coordinate long-running or multi-step business workflow state

pieces.label: Workflow/orchestration layer such as Step Functions where appropriate

questions.explanation: A maintainable enterprise design separates identity/authorization, the application API contract, workflow orchestration, and model runtime invocation. That keeps clients decoupled from model-specific changes and gives each layer an explicit security/operational responsibility. Archive storage and DNS routing can matter elsewhere, but they do not replace these integration roles.
hints: Separate who is allowed, how clients integrate, how workflow state is coordinated, and where model inference happens.

questions.prompt: Complete the Bedrock streaming call. The surrounding code already shows how the event stream is consumed; type the full invocation expression that belongs on the right-hand side.
questions.explanation: ConverseStream is the Bedrock Runtime conversational streaming API. It returns an event stream, so the application processes events such as contentBlockDelta as they arrive rather than waiting for the full response. This question deliberately makes you reconstruct the useful call instead of merely recalling the word “stream”; production code still needs throttling/transient-error handling and to handle the event types it expects.
hints: Use the streaming counterpart of Converse, with the model ID and already-built messages.

questions.prompt: A browser request crosses an application API, Lambda, a retrieval call, Bedrock, and an enterprise tool. Some requests fail intermittently. Select the evidence that directly helps reconstruct one failing execution across those layers.

evidence.label: A request/correlation ID propagated through application logs and downstream calls
Distributed trace spans / per-stage timing for the failing request
Bedrock invocation status/error metadata and the model/prompt version used
Retrieved document/chunk IDs and retrieval/tool outcomes for the same request
Monthly Cost Explorer totals with no request-level correlation
Route 53 query logs for an unrelated marketing domain
The AMI ID of an unrelated EC2 instance

questions.explanation: Intermittent cross-service failures are easiest to reproduce when one request can be followed end to end. Correlation/trace IDs join application and dependency evidence; model/prompt identity plus Bedrock status explains the inference stage; and retrieval/tool outcomes show whether the wrong context or a downstream action failed. Aggregate cost and unrelated DNS/AMI data cannot localize a single execution.
hints: Select evidence that can be tied to the same failing request, not merely the same month or account.
